Input: Why doesn't Ukraine hit Moscow every time the Soviets hit Kiev? Yesterday, Ukrainian drones attacked targets in 5 regions of Russia, including Moscow, with Russian officials reporting that they shot down 2 drones. Radio ‘Svoboda’ found the position of the air defense systems that shot down the drone in the Kuchino district in Balashikha near Moscow. The air defense system is located at the Kuchino landfill. Using Google maps, journalist Mark Krutov compiled a map of the locations of anti-aircraft systems. He has been doing it since May 2023, when the attacks on Moscow began. If you remember, in May 2023 drones managed to hit the roof of the building inside the Kremlin wall in Moscow, targeting the Russian flag on top of it. Then, offices of Russian ministries had been attacked in the Moscow City. At one stage, the Moscow authorities sent policemen to guard the air space, whose job was to inform the ministry of defence. Then the policemen were given anti-drone guns. For weeks in 2023, Moscow airports had to halt operations for hours because of danger of drone attacks. Now, it appears that Ukraine resumed drone attacks on targets in the Moscow region. We know that Russian anti-air defence systems are the primary goals for Ukraine. If they are eliminated, it will give Ukraine the ability to hit military targets in the Moscow region. Let’s see how it goes in the next few weeks.

What are some major Soviet/Russian war crimes? The most horrible Russian war crimes are happening right now — most heinous crimes are committed by Russia’s army in Ukraine against Ukrainians, whom Kremlin propagandists still cynically call “a brotherly people.” There are over 100,000 war crimes recorded by the team of international war crimes prosecutors. Oleksii Kretsu, a Ukrainian soldier from Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine, spent nearly 2 years in Russian captivity. He recently was exchanged in a POW exchange and returned to Ukraine. He returned infected by tuberculosis and hepatitis B, contracted while in a Russian prison. His recollection of the time in Russian captivity sounds like a storyline of a horror film. “As soon as they removed the restraints from our hands and the blindfolds from our eyes, they gave us a ‘welcome’ – beating us with shockers, batons, hands, feet, and anything else they could get hold of.” “The treatment was terrible, and the conditions were horrific, simply unbearable. Every single day during the morning check, we were humiliated. The same shocker was used on us without hesitation.” “In the morning, from wake-up at 6:00 AM to 10:10 AM, we stood motionless in the cell. You stand facing the door: you can't even lower your head because they consider you to be sleeping. Each cell had surveillance cameras, usually two… Every movement was monitored.” “In winter, if it was -10 degrees outside, the cell temperature was, at best, 10-12 degrees Celsius. The small cells were mostly unheated during winter. We had to stand for hours in thin prison clothes, motionless, without any movement.” “They fed us grains soaked in boiling water and often in cold water. The only thing that tasted good was jelly with a piece of white bread. They also gave us mashed potatoes made from greenish potatoes, which were salad-colored.” “They also beat us during interrogations. I'm just a simple border guard, not an assault trooper, not a marine, not a machine gunner. And even then, I lost half of my teeth during these interrogations. What they did to the machine gunners or snipers is terrifying to imagine.” Oleksandr Hrytsiuk from Kivertsi, Volyn region, was captured in April 2022. In January 2024, his wife was informed that his body had been returned from captivity. When his wife arrived in Kyiv for body identification, she was shocked by what she saw. “It was a very horrifying sight. What struck me the most was how emaciated the body was.” The pathologist said that Oleksandr’s body weighed less than 50 kilograms. He was tall — 180 cm, and before captivity, he weighed 110 kg and was physically healthy. “What was left of him were just bones and skin. His head was all bruised, his nose was crooked, and his index fingers had no nails. Whether they were ripped out or smashed, I do not know. There were signs of torture all over his body,” his wife says. Some of his cellmates survived and later later told the story how they were tortured. Every day they were beaten — either in the cell or taken out of the cell to interrogation chambers. The Russians beat Ukrainian prisoners brutally, and Oleksandr was their prime target, because he was tall, he was from western Ukraine, and didn’t want to speak Russian. The guards barely fed them, sometimes even just threw them some dog food mixed with dog hair. “They called him a ‘Banderite’, saying all Banderites must be killed and cut to pieces. He was beaten very cruelly, to the point of losing consciousness. Between beatings, they were forced to stand motionless for hours, sometimes with their hands raised.” This is only a small part of Russian war crimes. There are many more details on terrifying conditions of Ukrainian POWs in Russian captivity. Please read and spread the word.

When is Putin going to see sense and note that his conventional military forces can’t take Ukraine let alone a NATO member? This question is 2 years and 4 months old: it was asked on April 16, 2022 — less than 2 months after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In over 2 years, Putin hasn’t figured out that his war is doomed — and keeps destroying Russia, its past, present and future. Russia has lost its reputation of a strong military power, lost hundreds of thousands of men on the battlefield (and millions to emigration), destabilized and cannibalized its economy, wasted enormous human and material resources, got pushed out of its most lucrative international markets, exhausted its already worn out and under-maintained infrastructure, with no ability to afford capital investment. In July 2024, Russia managed to gain more territory (red dots) — and lost 50,000 men doing that. The situation looks even more pointless for Russia if we look at the larger map. In fact, Russia still controls about the same percentage of the Ukrainian territory as in December 2022 — and much less than 2 years ago. Russia’s territorial gains of “800 square km” in 2024, which the Russian ministry of defence brags about, should be viewed to scale — Ukraine is 603,628 square km in size. 800 square km is 0.13%. To gain it, Russia has lost 200,000 men. 2.5 years after the start of the full-scale war, Russia is still unable to gain the full control of Donetsk region — the goal that Putin announced since day 1. 2.5 years!! At this rate, Russia will reach the borders of the Donetsk region in a few decades, having burned down its entire male population. With every month, Russia has to throw in more men than before — but the gains are getting smaller, not bigger. There are many reasons for that, including the quality of new recruits — it dropped substantially since the start of the war, as well as increased sophistication of the warfare — by now, drones became the leading defense tool for Ukraine, and Russia is unable to keep up the pace. The war that Putin refuses to stop is eating Russia from the inside like cancer. The Russian Federation wanted to absorb Ukraine, but in the process started eating itself. If Russia doesn’t lose any of its territories as the result of this war, I’ll be very surprised.

What if the Kursk disaster in 2000 had prevented Putin from getting to power? How would Russia have looked today? Vladimir Putin’s presidential term started with Kursk nuclear submarine disaster on 12 August 2000. The submarine sank in the Barents Sea and all 118 personnel on board perished. The crews of nearby ships, which all were taking part in a large-scale naval exercise, felt two explosions, but the generals did not start any search for the vessel for 6 hours. The explosion was so powerful, it was recorded by seismologists in Alaska. It took over 16 hours to locate the submarine (the emergency rescue buoy had been switched off). It was finally located on the ocean floor at a depth of 108 metres (354 ft). Newly inaugurated Putin was on holiday and refused to cut his vacation short, to deal with the crisis. After the explosions, 23 sailors remained alive on the submarine — they died waiting to be rescued. Putin was refusing to allow foreigners to be part of the rescue mission, and Russians were unable to do what was needed to be done. Desperate relatives were waiting for news about their men at the quayside, growing more and more despondent because of the inaction by the state officials and the Navy. All this time Russian officials lied about what was happening. “The communication with the crew has been established, they are getting hot food!” was telling the Navy spokesman. Blatant lies. Only on August 20 — 8 days after the catastrophe — the Norwegian vessel ‘Seaway Eagle’ was allowed to begin working on the recovery mission. Norwegian divers did in 24 hours what the Russians could not do in a week — they managed to open the submarine's emergency escape hatch. But it was too late. All survivors of the accident were already dead. When the Russian TV — which was still reporting freely at the time — done an investigative piece on the tragedy and showed the widows of the marines, Putin accused the program in ”hiring whores for $10” to discredit him: “You hire whores on purpose. You gave them 10 dollars each, specifically to discredit me,” Putin claimed. It was after the Kursk disaster that Putin began raider seizures of the independent media. This was 24 years ago. Today, the words “Kursk” and “Putin” are again in the news, but this time it’s the Kursk region of Russia — and the Ukrainian troops’ incursion into Russia. And once again, Putin is lying about it. But this no longer surprises anyone. ”Kursk” disaster didn’t cripple Putin’s grasp on power — but maybe, Kursk will?

How would the provision of Patriot air defence systems affect the situation in the city of Kharkiv? More than 10% of the population of Kharkiv (160,000 people) have lost their homes, 5 thousand buildings suffered damages or have been destroyed by the Russian artillery, missiles and bombs. If Kharkiv had effective air defence systems like Patriots, with sufficient munitions for them, this wouldn’t have happened. The White House administration has finally approved the use of American air defence systems to shoot down Russian planes over the Russian territory — that’s where they drop their guided bombs, which fall on Kharkiv and nearby towns. The new direction on the use of the U.S. weapons will allow Ukraine to employ American weapons to intercept Russian missiles that are targeting Kharkiv, and to attack concentrations of Russian troops just over the border in the vicinity of the city. This will allow for Ukraine to aim for high value targets such as command and control centers, artillery, logistics and air defence units that are located on Russian territory near Kharkiv and concentrating or rehearsing future operations against Ukraine. Russian propagandists must be devastated. No instruction manuals have been received from the AP (administration of the president) as yet, so they are keeping num about it.

What are the impacts of the fires at the Proletarsk oil depot in Russia on the environment? The fire at the strategic oil depot in the ARussian town of Proletarsk in Rostov region has been burning for 9 days, and almost all fuel had burnt out. (Video in the comments below.) But despite the smoke tail of 60 km long, the local enviromental control authorities assured residents that the quality of air was fine. Notwithstanding, the annual celebration of the Day of the City got cancelled by the administration, as well as all other outdoor activities — even though it’s the 100-year-anniversary of the district. The district administration's press service stated that the festivities were cancelled due to "the current situation in the district." (“The situation” is also the word used by Vladimir Putin to describe the Ukrainian invasion of Russia in the Kursk region.) Residents of Proletarsk complain that they have "no air to breathe" and are buying up masks to breathe filtered air. Locals are afraid to eat the vegies from their gardens: when they wash them, the water turns black. Compared to the first week of the fire, it looks like the flames are getting smaller, expectedly, as not much fuel is left. The fire began as the result of the Ukrainian drone attack on August 18. After 4 days, the local authorities even called priests to perform a prayer service, asking for divine assistance in putting out the flames. The prayers didn’t work; attempts to control the fire by firemen also didn’t work. Over 40 firemen got injured. The fuel depot had 74 giant tanks storing different types of fuel, including specific types of aviation kerosine. Russia’s ministry of emergency situations that controls the fire service didn’t post any information about the raging fire in Proletarsk, which was visible on satellite photos. The reason for the silence — not to give information to the Ukrainian Telegram channels, which would celebrate their success. At the beginning of the war, it was Russia that was destroying oil depots in Ukraine with missile strikes. Ukraine is simply paying back.

Is Russia’s talk of Ukraine using a dirty bomb on its own territory indicate that Russia may be planning to use a dirty bomb themselves and blame it on Ukraine? ‘Russia Today’, TASS, and RIA Novosti, as well as all the Putin’s shills are posting and reposting each other, threatening that “Ukraine is going to blow a dirty bomb in Eastern Europe.” Is Russia going to blow a dirty bomb somewhere and blame it on Ukraine? Hell, no. Putin is embarrassed that his troops can’t stop the Ukrainian offensive in the Kursk region, and it makes him look pathetic. So, Putin’s administration is trying to eclipse the global news about Ukraine’s success in invading Russia by scaremongering: even if no one believes that Ukraine would drop a “dirty bomb”, they might start worrying that it’s Putin who is planning to do it, and the incessant chatter is the Kremlin’s coverup tactic. To remind you: Russians have done it before, they’ve threatened a “Ukrainian dirty bomb”, to overshadow undesirable news. Putin’s propagandists are terrified to try something new in a crisis — in case it doesn’t work and the author of the idea moves next in line for a hexa-share Lefortovo cell. That’s why Russian propagandists prefer to reapply tried and tested methods: dirty bomb, bio laboratories, WW3 — and so on, ad nauseam. Because it would be stupid to make nuclear threats in the current situation — Russia is being invaded right now! It would be time to walk the walk — not talk the talk, if Russia’s nuclear blackmail were even 0.5% truthful. Even Medvedev — who loves nuclear bluff — had shut up, and is only squealing about “illegal border crossing” and “terroristic nature of the neo-Nazi regime” (yes, for real). So, what’s next on the list, after the nukes? “A dirty bomb” — sounds just as worrisome. Just another PR caper by Kremlin shills.

What is your analysis of the satellite images of the Ukrainian Defence Intelligence drone strikes on the Russian radar station in Orenburg Oblast? On May 26, a long-range Ukrainian drone attacked an over-the-horizon radar station in Russia in Orenburg region — at a distance of more than 1,800 km. Orsk is located 140 km further from the front line in Ukraine than the Bashkir city of Salavat, which was previously the furthest location from Ukraine attacked by Ukrainian drones in Russia. The drone targeted the Voronezh-M missile attack warning radar station in the village of Gorkovskoye near the town of Orsk in Orenburg region. The station is fairly new — it was commissioned in 2017. 2 days ago, Ukraine already hit another Voronezh-DM radar station, located in the Krasnodar Territory. “Voronezh” type stations are designed to detect and track ballistic and cruise missiles and other aerodynamic objects at distances up to 6,000 These long-range radar stations are part of Russia’s “strategic umbrella”. Since 2011, these radar stations became part of Russia’s Aerospace Defense Forces. It is these stations that Russia is using to hit targets in Ukraine. Like the attack on Kharkiv hypermarket last Saturday.

Has Putin already decided to attack NATO? Putin can’t attack NATO countries while he’s stuck in the war of attrition in Ukraine. But if Putin is allowed to take over Ukraine — or “freeze” the war on current separation lines, with Ukraine being forced to de-arm and the ability of Russia to mobilize soldiers from the occupied Ukrainian territories (which they already do), then the chance of Putin attacking Baltics increases tenfold. And vice versus, if Russia is decisively defeated in Ukraine, the threat of Putin attacking a NATO country in Europe will drop close to 0%. Russia will not be able to recover quickly and Europe will have enough time to prepare an impenetrable defense. Putin won’t have the resources to attack the Baltic countries or Poland, if he suffers defeat and his army is destroyed in Ukraine. That’s why the most logical course of action for the European allies of Ukraine is to send Ukrainians enough weapons to destroy Putin’s army in Ukraine, so he cannot even think about an attack on Europe. Then these weapons that are stored in the warehouses won’t be needed in the future.

What do you make of the fact that Paul Whelan was left out of the prisoner exchange between the US and Russia? In December 2022, Paul Whelan wasn’t part of a prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. — instead, American basketball player Brittney Greener was traded for Russian arms dealer Victor Bout. Since then, there weren’t exchanges that were made public. Exchanges are never straightforward and who gets back is determined not only by what one side desires but also whom the opposition is prepared to exchange. Victor Bout, Brittney Griner. Putin managed to get his “merchant of death” Bout back, releasing an American hostage Griner who was arrested in Russia for carrying vaporizer cartridges containing less than a gram of hash oil. Russia accused her in possession of illegal drugs and sentenced for 9 years of prison. While possessing marijuana is illegal in Russia, the whole arrest and sentencing of Griner were handled with such media frenzy and promotion by Russian propagandists and the Kremlin bots online that it looked like a special operation to pressure the American side to release a well-connected arms dealer — by the end of 2022, Putin desperately needed someone experienced in that particular sector. Why Paul Whelan wasn’t exchanged at the time was asked by many, and the answer is that maybe Russia wanted someone else in exchange to Whelan whom the FSB insists was a real spy. Security professional Paul Whelan was arrested in Moscow in 2018 and accused of being a spy. Whelan said he had been in Russia for a friend's wedding. Before 2008, Whelan served as a Marine, and after his discharge was working as a security chief for a commercial organization. He visited Russia several times before and the wedding he was planning to attend was of a fellow marine. Whelan says he was given the hard drive by a Russian friend in what he now he now believes was a “sting operation” — Russia accused the drive contained some classified intel and sentenced him to 16 years imprisonment. This week, after several Russian political prisoners disappeared from their prisons in Russia, it was discovered that Paul Whelan is also missing. So are Putin’s critics journalist Maria Ponomarenko and an opposition politician Vladimir Kara-Murza. More confirmations are coming from Russia that a big prisoner exchange deal is in the works. Maybe this time Paul Whelan will also be released.

What do you think about Bellingcat's analysis that the missile that hit Okhmatdyt Children's Hospital in Kyiv was a Kh-101 missile? Bellingcat has one of the most thorough and methodical investigative teams. It were them who found a guy responsible for the poisoning of Alexei Navalny — Bellingcat managed to find his mobile phone number and cleverly dropped enough details of the crime that convinced the culprit to confess over the phone. It was the Bellingcat team who found a link between the trips of Russian GRU agents from the “assassin team” and episodes of “Havana Syndrome” among employees of the USA embassies around the world. On July 9, 2024, Bellingcat released their report on identifying the missile that hit the largest Ukrainian children’s hospital ‘Okhmatdyt’ on July 8 concluding with certainty — including the geolocated images — that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile that deliberately targeted the civilian medical facility, debunking Russia’s claim that it was a Norway-supplied air defense missile. Woefully for Russia, the moment of a strike was captured by a Ukrainian onlooker on video, showing the arrival of the missile and the sound accompanying it. An enhanced image showing the missile that hit the children’s hospital in Kyiv. Several international military experts identified the missile as Kh-101 that only Russia uses. Although the Ukrainian side only released the images of the parts of the missile, found in the rubble, Bellingcat researchers found a photo taken by a journalist at the site that matches the photos of the missile wreckage released by the Ukrainian side. But the most profound admission of Russia’s guilt came from none other as the UN rep for RF, Vasily Nebenzya. Without lifting eyes from the paper in front of him, Nebenzya proclaimed that if it were indeed a Russian missile that hit Okhmatdyt, “nothing would have remained of the building, and all the people in it would have died.” It’s a blatant and moronic lie. Nebenzya cannot not know that — he denied Russia’s strikes on civilian targets many times before — and still, he duly reads the lies that are given to him. This moronic lie is yet another proof that it was Russia that hit the children’s hospital — and they targeted the medical clinic for seriously sick kids deliberately.

Is the West now negotiating with Putin or is it too vain? Putin is seeking peace and has made an offer to negotiate on the basis of the current situation on the battlefield. So the ball is in Ukraine's court. Except for Kremlin bots, no one pays much attention to Putin’s blabbing anymore. At some stage, you no longer find it ridiculous or absurd, but can’t help feeling that you see a seriously mentally disturbed individual who needs professional help. Putin keeps saying the same things in his speeches most of the time, and the only reason people took notice of his yesterday’s “peace proposal” to Ukraine was because Putin demanded that Ukraine withdrew from the territories it controls — and just gave them to Russia. In fact, Putin’s demand to give him the city of Kherson is probably the first case in the history of mankind when an invader demands to give him the territory from which his own army fled in disgrace. Just imagine. 1943. Germany is stuck on the eastern front in Ukraine. And here the Fuhrer proposes: alright, we are ready to negotiate, but only if the Red Army first withdraws beyond the Urals — and right up to the Urals there will be Nazi Reich. That’s the value of Putin’s “peace proposal”, in a nutshell. In fact, anyone calling Putin’s ultimatum “a peace plan” is either on Kremlin’s payout or have their own agenda: invading someone’s country and then demanding to keep their land is a “peace plan” to the same degree as mugging someone at gunpoint is a “business plan.” Putin's requests about Ukraine’s surrender haven’t been discussed at the G7 summit and were not taken seriously, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz said in an interview with ZDF. Not sure how soon the exhausted mind of Vladimir Putin will have a chance to get the professional help it needs, but Putin’s loss of touch with reality hasn’t affected these around him to the same extent. In the occupied Crimea, Russians are getting ready to do a runner: the heads of Crimean museums received letters from the Ministry of Culture, ordering them to prepare museum valuables for “evacuation.” Putin may be putting up a brave front, but his officials are busy looting and stealing what they can, before they are kicked out of Crimea. Except for Putin, everyone understands what is going to happen next.

What can we learn from the region around Kursk, scene of a famous Soviet counter-offensive in 1943, to understand the scale of the disaster inflicted on Russia by Vladimir Putin? Russia-Ukraine war is full of symbols. Startling success of Ukraine’s offensive in the Kursk region — the scene of 1943 milestone battle of the WW2, where the Soviet army trashed Nazi troops — is one of such omens. Some western speakers make an obtuse mistake when talking about “Russia defeating Hitler” in WW2 — it wasn’t Russia but the Soviet Union. To understand the difference, bear in mind that when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, more Soviet citizens were living outside Russia, than in Russia itself. By the same token, the Soviet effort against Nazi troops in WW2 also included more non-Russians than Russians. The second largest republic of the USSR was Ukraine — which was nearly fully occupied by Hitler in WW2, so the 7 millions Ukrainians in the Soviet Army really fought for the right to return to their homes. 1943 Battle of Kursk was the largest tank battle in history. It involved 6,000 tanks, 2,000,000 troops, and 4,000 aircraft. The USSR had 3,600 tanks, which was only made possible because of massive material support from the USA and UK. Without the American ‘Lend Lease’, the Soviet army wouldn’t be able to function at the level it needed to be. The Kursk battle dealt a final blow to German forces on the eastern front and decisively turned the tide of World War 2. Hitler troops lost the initiative, which they have never regained. So, the Kursk battle in WW2 was a turning point when the Nazis lost so badly, they never managed to recover. Soviets were proud of the Kursk battle (“Kursk Curve” in the Soviet history books). But for Vladimir Putin, the word “Kursk” is anything but pleasant. On August 12, 2000, Russian submarine “Kursk” sank, with Putin’s government screwing up the rescue effort, and all survivors aboard ending up dead. The people were especially shocked by the fact that Putin refused to return from his Black Sea vacation as the catastrophe was unfolding. On August 12, 2024, as the Ukrainian offensive in the Kursk region was progressing, president Zelenskyy said: ”We see how Russia really moves in the times of Putin: 24 years ago, there was the Kursk disaster – the symbolic beginning of his rule; and now we can see what the end for him is. And that is Kursk as well.” For superstitious Putin, the 2nd Kursk disaster must be petrifying — Putin certainly didn’t look confident at the latest briefing of Russia’s Security Council. For a long time, Putin was bragging about “Russia’s victory against Hitler”, completely denying credit to the allies (the U.S., UK, and others) and the input of other Soviet republics, including Ukraine. This time, Ukraine, backed by its allies (the U.S., UK, and others) is standing against fascist Russia — and the battlefield is once again in Kursk. This moment, no doubt, will be one of the focal points of the Russia-Ukraine war in future history books.

Which country has better military technology, Ukraine or Russia/USSR? Ukraine is the first country in the world to create a new branch of the armed forces — Unmanned Systems Forces. The Unmanned Systems Forces use air, sea, and ground unmanned and robotic systems in their combat operations. The drone-making industry of Ukraine is diverse and competitive: the Ukrainian army is purchasing drones from 120 local manufacturers. Colonel Vadym Sukharevskyi was appointed as the Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces. He is one of the first commanders of the AFU, who began to effectively use aerial drones in combat operations. Sukharevski was also behind Ukraine producing novel electronic warfare devices using his own technology. Ukraine is changing the rules of war through innovation and technology, putting emphasis on the use of drones. Russia still heavily relies on “meat waves”, trying to compensate for its technological weakness.

What do you think of Russian Finance Ministry's projection of a budget deficit of 0.8% of Russia’s GDP for 2024? The Russian federal budget deficit for January - April of this year amounted to 3.963 trillion ruble (USD $39 billion), the Federal Treasury of the Russian Federation reported. In early May 2024, Russia’s Ministry of Finance said there would be a deficit of 1.5 trillion ruble ($15 billion) — that’s 260% of the predicted figure. The whole annual budget deficit was supposed to be only 1.6 trillion rub. ($16 billion). Only the deficit of January-April 2024 makes 1.8% of Russia’s GDP. So, they are running short of money for sure. The only way to compensate for that is to get much higher income during the remaining months of the year. What can be expected next: That’s why Putin really needs to freeze the war in Ukraine. The Russian economy is working in the crisis mode for 2.5 years. Things start going wrong right, left and centre. Any major issue can become the proverbial “last straw”.

What are some positive aspects of Russian culture and its people? Russian military correspondents are furious: residents of Kursk region are evacuating, instead of queuing to sign up as volunteers for the Russian army. (Video in the comments below.) “What the heck??” barks a Russian man dressed in a military uniform. “As males, you should be defending your homes, you should be delivering food to our guys, or digging trenches — or if you can’t do it, just give your cars to our guys, so they can use them at the front. Why are you just driving away??” For 25 years, since Putin took helm in Russia, the state was training citizens to be passive: “They at the top know best what to do”, “we are just small people”, “we can’t change anything”. People have learned to don’t have any opinions of their own, because having an opinion can get you in trouble. They’ve learned to “stay out of politics”, learned to live by the motto, “my hut is at the edge of the village, I don’t know anything”. Putin’s administration chose to downplay “the situation in Kursk region” and Russian propagandists are now saying that “Ukraine made a foolish move” and “everything is under control, situation stabilized, no losses.” Kursk residents know it’s not true — they can look out of the window and see what happens, but because the state tells them “it’s all good”, they simply do what they feel is the right thing for them — run away. They don’t want to defend Putin’s regime, they don’t want to fight and possibly die defending their homeland. It’s weird, but there are no public protests in Russian towns taken over by the Ukrainian forces, as there were in spring 2022 when the Russian army invaded Ukrainian cities and thousands of Ukrainians went to town squares to protest against the Russian invaders — Ukrainian men, women, elders, kids were standing with bare hands against armed Russian soldiers, yelling at them, “Go home!!” “Occupiers, go home!” — protests in Kherson in March 2022. Similar mass protests were happening in many other Ukrainian towns captured by the Russian army. People in Kherson were standing with Ukrainian flags, with anti-Putin and anti-Russia posters, against armed Russians and military vehicles. Russians don’t protest. They seem to be indifferent to what is happening around them. They realized their officials lie to them — they knew it all along, but it was safer to pretend they believed them — and they have no idea what is real and what is not anymore, they just don’t trust anybody — but pretend to trust the guys who are in charge right now. If Ukrainians are in charge, they pretend to trust Ukrainians. If Russians are in charge, they pretend to trust Russians. Russian citizens have no opinions of their own — or if they do, they keep them buried so deep, they themselves are terrified to admit they have them. It’s not a “slave mentality” — it’s learned helplessness. They really think there is nothing they can do that will change anything. Obviously, this aspect of the modern Russian culture and collective psyche is highly beneficial to the advancing Ukrainian army, which doesn’t have to deal with hostile population. Rather, Ukrainians are dealing with passive, yet quietly curious population, compliant and eager to follow instructions. Russian State Duma member Vitaly Milonov called on men from the Kursk region to sign contracts with the Ministry of Defense and defend their homeland on their own — obviously, Putin isn’t going to send to Kursk reinforcements from the front in Ukraine, where he’s sending most troops and equipment. Milonov, too, believes that only women, children and the elderly should be evacuating from Kursk, but local men should take on the defense of border areas. “No one has to do anything for Russian residents of border regions,” announced Milonov — they themselves must show that they can defend their land. With such an attitude from the Russian state, no wonder that Ukrainians keep taking over several more settlements every day. Isn’t it weird that Russians are willing to go to Ukraine “to make Russia great again” (and be paid “big wages”) — but have no desire or interest to defend their own homes?

Why do you think the Russian government has refused to open a criminal investigation into the death of Alexei Navalny? The Russian state officially announced they wouldn’t be investigating the death of oppositionist Alexei Navalny — naturally, the FSB doesn’t want anyone near the obvious murder case, implicating Putin’s regime. Apparently, Navalny became unwell during his morning walk. He complained of a sharp stomach pain. He was taken back to the solo punishment cell by the guards, where he was thrown for some “violation”. It was the 27th time Navalny was in a solo punishment cell, usually this would be a 14-day punishment. He was found unresponsive in his cell later by guards and taken to medical quarters, an ambulance was called, but couldn’t revive him. A day before his death Navalny participated in a video hearing of his complaint and was in good spirits, appearing healthy. 2 days before his death, his parents visited him in prison, and also reported he was feeling well. The details on the actual circumstances of Navalny’s death were apparently reported by some guards or other prisoners through connections that his friend, investigator Christo Grozev, and other anti-Putin Russians in exile have within the Russian prison system. Is it true that wages in Russia are very low and the cost of living is very high? A young Russian policewoman was fired for posting a reel on Instagram where she mocked her $400 (40,000 rub.) monthly salary, which is actually less than $100 per week. (Video in the comments below.) 28-year-old Olga Gaidukova worked as a district police officer in the town of Novocherkassk (Rostov region), population 160,000, which is in the South of Russia, near the Ukrainian border. The satiric reel about her salary, which she published in her personal Instagram account, scored a lot of views and likes. It is this popularity that got her in trouble. Reportedly, the young lady was called to her superiors, who demanded from her to delete the Instagram account — but she refused and was fired. The defiant ex-police officer admitted that she didn’t think her bosses would go that far. There aren’t too many willing candidates for such jobs and police officers are overworked. The cost of living keeps skyrocketing. Mortgage rates are at 17% in Russia, and the government just cancelled special rates for first home buyers (which were at 8%). “Prices are cheaper than they will be tomorrow!” — Russians bitterly joke about the constantly rising prices. The Russian central bank plans to raise the base rate, which is currently at 16%, so the mortgage rates could be going beyond the scary 17% per year already this month. Putin keeps saying that Russians can purchase more goods with their low salaries than westerners can buy with their much higher wages, but I don’t think many westerners would want to live on the ration of cabbage soup with bread and tea with cookies. This is actually what pensioners in Russia eat every day, because most of their pension money they spend on utilities bills (aka “kommunalka”). After paying for their homes, they can only spend $1–3 per day on food. And no, it’s not enough to buy proper food. Yes, Russian people working regular jobs live better than homeless people in America living in the streets. But they don’t live anywhere as comfortable as Americans who work in the same type of jobs. That’s a fact.

Is it true that Vladimir Putin brought a Labrador to a meeting with Angela Merkel because she's afraid of dogs? In January 2007, during the meeting with Angela Merkel in Sochi, Putin brought in his Labrador in front of the German Chancellor, who has a phobia of dogs. The episode attracted so much bad publicity that Putin began explaining himself to foreign media, starting 2016. His version is that “he didn’t know” and “everybody in the office loved the dog” that had been, according to Putin’s version, always casually walking around the residence. Since then, the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti re-published the story explaining that Putin “didn’t do it to cause harm” several times — on February 20, 2022, for instance, 4 days before Russia invaded Ukraine. Merkel refuted Putin’s explanation that “he didn’t know” about her phobia of dogs. Merkel visited Moscow, Russia, after being elected chancellor in 2005, where she met with Putin, and he told her that he knew about her “dog problem” — and presented her with a big plush toy of a dog. “Even then, Putin told me that he had heard about my problems with dogs, and gave me this huge stuffed dog,” recalls Merkel. It was during that meeting in Sochi in 2007 that Putin told Merkel for the first time that he considered the collapse of the USSR to be the most terrible event of the 20th century. And she replied that for her it was a happy moment in her life, which allowed her to freely control her destiny.

Am I right in thinking the great Ukrainian Peace conference in Switzerland has turned out to be a massive flop and a waste of time? Definitely a slap in Putin’s face, after his pathetic ultimatum, “just give me your land, because we have utterly failed to take it by force”.

Could this be true? Russian newspaper: 17,000 Wagner soldiers from prisons killed on the battlefield. What do people in Russia know about this? Is the truth hidden for Russians? These losses exceed the total number of killed in action during the 10 years of the USSR invasion of Afghanistan. Most fighters recruited by ‘Wagner’ from prisons were sent into “meat assaults” near Bakhmut — and 17,000 of them died there. the Battle of Bakhmut lasted 327 days, from July 15, 2022, till June 6, 2023. During this time: 35% of recruited prisoners (1 in 3) died. In the Battle of Bakhmut, Russian forces captured 677 sq. km of territory(261 square miles). 29 dead soldiers for each 1 square km. When recruiting inmates in prisons, Yevgeny Prigozhin told them that they would’t be just “cannon fodder”, but would serve as equals with the other mercenaries. But the casualties data show that it wasn’t the case: the share of “free mercenaries” among these killed in action is only 12%. Before the start of the Battle of Bakhmut and recruiting in prisons (March-June 2022), Wagner lost only 300 men. ’Mediazona’ determined the number of deaths by the records of payments to families of the deceased. (The journalists got hold of Wagner’s financial documentation, and then cross-referenced it with databases on inheritance, presidential pardons, court verdicts, etc.) ‘Wagner’ recruiters went through 617 Russian prisons and penal colonies, where they recruited over 48,000 convicted criminals. The majority of them were pulled from maximum security prisons. After the aborted ‘Wagner’ coup in June 2023, Russian authorities tried to bury ‘Wagner’ into oblivion. But “meat assault” tactics, first used in Ukraine by Prigozhin, are now implemented by regular Russian infantry units, as well as units made of inmates. To compare, the project UALosses, which calculates military losses by Ukraine, recorded that 4,871 Ukrainians (confirmed with names) were killed in the Battle of Bakhmut from July 15, 2022 to June 6, 2023. (The actual number is likely higher, up to 8,000.) But there were not only ‘Wagner’ mercenaries involved in the operation in Bakhmut, regular Russian troops had been there as well. So, proportionately, Russian losses are likely to be no less than 3:1 in Bakhmut, or higher. But it doesn’t seem that losses among prisoners — or even deaths of Russia’s contract soldiers or mobilized — are a worry for the Russian populace. Putin’s propaganda machine turned into a death cult where perishing in the war of conquest in the name of “Great Russia” is publicly glorified — while no one actually cares about the disabled vets or families who lost fathers, husbands, and sons. Most Russians don’t care — as long as they can keep living their lives, pretending that nothing happens.

Is the president of Ukraine banning Christianity and closing churches in his country? Yesterday, the Ukrainian parliament voted to ban the FSB Moscow church in Ukraine — after 2.5 years of the full-scale war and 10.5 years since Russia annexed Crimea. But finally, it’s done! By no means it means that “Ukraine bans Christianity”. All Christian confessions — including the Orthodox Christianity — are allowed in Ukraine, none are being “banned”. What is severed, however, is the churches subordination to Moscow Patriarchate. It’s been long overdue, but after much deliberation and explanatory work to Christians worldwide, the Ukrainian lawmakers finally voted to approve it. Since the beginning of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, many Moscow-appointed priests were acting on orders of their FSB curators. As of May 2024, Ukraine still had about 8,000 communities that were part of the Moscow Patriarchate. Now these communities will have to cut ties with Moscow, and join Ukraine's own Christian Orthodox Church, which had been created in 2018 and blessed by the Holy Synod of the Patriarchate of Constantinople, the worldwide leadership of Orthodox Christianity. In 2022-2023, about 1,000 communities have already disassociated from Moscow and joined the Orthodox Church of Ukraine. Once again: the law gives 9 months to all Christian Orthodox communities to cut the ties to Moscow. What happens if they don’t? Then the government and the church have to go to court, and it will probably take years until any orders are given as to what to do with these communities. These churches will not be shut down and will continue operating until such time the court makes its determination. The Ukrainian government obviously understands that it’s a sensitive matter and acts in good faith, yet with full realization of the fact that it has the utmost obligation to protect the national security. In fact, it wasn’t Ukraine that cancelled the Russian church in its country. By invading Ukraine and killing tens of thousands of Ukrainians, it was Russia that “cancelled” itself and its institutions in Ukraine.

Please feel free to add additional information on the topic if needed." Putin’s propagandists are getting utterly desperate. And because they are utterly desperate, they are making dumb mistakes. The USSR historians began calling it “Kievan Rus”, because in the Soviet history books the history of the USSR was starting with 9th century Rus. The legend of Kyiv being founded in 482 by brothers Kyi, Shchek, Khoryv and their sister Lybid was also included. By adopting the name “Rossia” (Russia) Muscovy princes laid their claim on the lands that belonged to Ukraine. 1709 newspaper “The Daily Courant” talks about Muscovy and Ukraine. The decision to change the name from the principality of Muscovy to the Russian Empire was political, and, as it was customary at the time, accompanied by forged history, backing the claim. The explosions were so powerful that they got picked by seismographs across the globe. The nearby 28,000-ton battlecruiser ‘Pyotr Velikiy’ shook from the 1st explosion. However, the Russian Navy didn’t acknowledge they had a major catastrophe. All 118 crew members aboard ‘Kursk’ perished, although 23 sailors survived the explosions and were alive for hours, hoping to be rescued. One of the ship’s officers, Lieutenant Captain Dmitri Koselnikov, left a note dated 2 hours after the 2nd explosion, saying there were 23 survivors. The submarine sank to the sea floor. The survivors barricaded themselves in a rear compartment and waited for a rescue. The rescue never came. ”Kursk”, a movie based on the disaster, starring Colin Firth, came out in 2018. As the disaster was unfolding, Vladimir Putin, the newly inaugurated president of Russia, continued his holidays on the Black Sea. Putin’s first statement about the submarine disaster was only made a week after. It took a week before a permission was granted to foreign countries to attempt a recovery mission (the Russian Navy failed to get into the sunk submarine) — and on August 21, a team of British and Norwegian divers accessed the vessel and found its entire crew dead. In 2000, the Russian media was still privately owned, so the coverage of how the Russian state handled the ‘Kursk’ disaster was sharply critical. Putin was furious over the ways TV amplified his haphazard response. He accused the TV producers in “hiring $10 whores” to pose as wives of deceased sailors, with the goal to portray him, Vladimir Putin, in a bad light. Kursk’s commanding officer, Gennady Lyachin; photo from 1999 parade. When questioned by relatives of the deceased on August 22, 2000, Putin put the blame on Russia’s “economic and military decline” before he came to power. It’s unlikely that there will be many mentions of the sunk ‘Kursk’ in the Russian media today. Not when Russia just suffered such a humiliating invasion by Ukraine last week, precisely in the Kursk region.

Can Ukraine make its own weapons? Ukraine can and does make its own weapons: Russia-Ukraine war of 2022–2024 is the first war in history where drones became the weapons that dominate the terrain. Within the last 2 years, drone production in Ukraine grew 100-fold. Since February 2022, Ukraine created and developed the UAV market from the ground up. One of such manufacturers are making drones called “Hornets”. There are smaller and larger FPV drones — “Wild Hornets”, “Queen Hornets”, as well as other models. All of them are Ukrainian-made. The Ukrainian drone operators have learned to use the same drone for many missions — a drone drops explosives and returns to the base, to get munitions. Drones are even used to retrieve weapons from the battlefield. Here you can see “Hornet Queen” picking weapons on the battlefield using a magnet. In December 2023, Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy set the task of producing a million drones for the Ukrainian Armed Forces. By now, the task has been completed, says Ukraine’s minister of digital transformation Mykhailo Fedorov. There are already contracts for the production of a million of drones for the Ukrainian army. They include standard FPV drones, long-range, reconnaissance and other types of drones that are already used by the Ukrainian defenders at the front. Just imagine this number: 1,000,000 drones! It’s 2 drones per each Russian soldier on the Ukrainian land. But tens of thousands of drones go directly from manufacturers to the Ukrainian units at the front without involving the government and the ministry of defense. They are paid for from donations that people make on behalf of certain units. So, if a certain unit requires more drones, they place a request with a manufacturer they know, and get a delivery within days, without the need for ministerial approvals. This is why the Ukrainian army is so much more efficient, and why the Russian soldiers say that it feels like the Ukrainians have 50:1 advantage in drones. This also saves thousands of Ukrainian lives.

What do you think will happen to Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich who was arrested for alleged spying in Russia? On July 19, 2024, the Regional Court in Yekaterinburg, Russia, sentenced American journalist Evan Gershkovich to 16 years in a maximum security colony. Russian human rights activist Vladimir Osechkin says that possibly he was baited by the FSB, to facilitate his arrest. 32-year-old journalist of WSJ was found guilty of espionage for collecting information about ‘Uralvagonzavod’, which is a factory that makes tanks for the Russian army. The prosecutor asked for an 18-year sentence. Gershkovich pleaded “not guilty” and insisted that he was acting as a journalist, not a spy. The court hearings were held behind closed doors, as the prosecution alleged the information that Gershkovich was getting was a “state secret”. Only the judge, the prosecutor, the defendant and his lawyers were present. Journalists were allowed into the meeting room for a few minutes before the hearing commenced to take photos and videos. Gershkovich, with a shaved head, greeted his colleagues with a smile, but did not answer any questions. Journalists were also allowed into the courtroom for the announcement of the harsh verdict: 16 years in a maximum security prison. Evan Gershkovich was detained on March 29, 2023 in Yekaterinburg, where he arrived for the second time in a month, to continue his investigation for the next story. At the WSJ Gershkovich worked since January 2022 — he joined the respected media just a month before Russia invaded Ukraine. Since then, he authored several key news stories related to Russia and Ukraine. In early March 2023, weeks before his arrest in Russia, he and his colleagues released a story about the growing tensions between the founder of “Wagner” Yevgeny Prigozhin and the Kremlin elites. In particular, the material stated, Kremlin officials turned to Russian President Vladimir Putin with a request to “rein in” Prigozhin, who criticized the Russian Ministry of Defense. Gershkovich was also one of the authors of a high-profile WSJ article about how Putin’s entourage may be hiding truthful information from him about the war in Ukraine. Putin receives a written report from the front every morning, however, the reports emphasize Russia army’s successes, and failures are tuned down. The reports are also delayed for several days, because they have to pass filters of the FSB and the Security Council, as well as get a personal stamp of approval from Nikolai Patrushev (then the secretary of Russia’s Security Council), the article claimed. Gershkovich's materials before his arrest in March 2023 were devoted to the worsening prospects for the Russian economy, the situation around Bakhmut, the visit to Moscow of China’s leader Xi Jinping and protests over the bill on "foreign agents" in Georgia. According to the photographer who worked with Gershkovich, he was collecting material for an article about how people in Russian regions perceive the war, for which he visited Yekaterinburg and Nizhny Tagil, and planned to go to other cities. The media wrote that Gershkovich was also interested in activities of the “Wagner”, including recruitment and cemeteries of the deceased fighters. At his court process, Gershkovich did not admit guilt and insisted that his research was purely journalistic. Evan Gershkovich became the first American journalist in modern Russian history to be accused of espionage. The last time an American journalist had been detained in Russia on espionage charges was in 1986, when a “News & World Report” employee Nicholas Daniloff was arrested. Daniloff was exchanged 3 weeks later. Before his arrest, Gershkovich worked in Russia for about 6 years, since 2017. At the time of his detainment, he had been living in London but regularly traveled on business trips to Russia, where he worked as part of the WSJ's Moscow bureau. His parents Mikhail Gershkovich and Emma Milman were emigrants from the USSR, but Evan himself lived his entire life in America. Several journalists who were friends with Gershkovich said that they warned him that reporting in Russia on the topics he was picking was dangerous and he could be arrested. But obviously, he didn’t think so. Gershkovich’s name has been frequently mentioned as someone who could be exchanged to Russian spies and assassins, arrested in Europe and the USA. He is probably the highest profile American hostage held by Putin. Putin discussed exchanging Gershkovich in his interview to Tucker Carlson in February 2024. Putin wanted to get in exchange the FSB assassin Vadim Krasikov, who is imprisoned in Germany. In 2021, Vadim Krasikov was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Chechen field commander Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin in 2019. Carlson said at the time that Putin needed to talk to Germans about it. Peculiarly, Gershkovich’s process wasn’t held in Moscow but 2 thousand kilometers away, in Yekaterinburg, where he was arrested — away from Russia’s capital, where most of the foreign correspondents reside. This obviously prevented many western ambassadors and embassy officials from attending the process, which they would likely do as a show of solidarity, if the court hearing was in Moscow. The only hope for Gershkovich to get out of the Russian prison is an agreement for an exchange, which Putin would probably only approve if his assassin Krasikov is released, and Germany doesn’t seem keen on that. Otherwise, Gershkovich may only hope to get out if Vladimir Putin, on whose order he was arrested (no doubt, such high profile arrest and prosecution would require the highest nod), is no longer the ruler of Russia. So, Gershkovich is likely to remain behind bars in Russia, as the locals call it, “for as long as Putin is alive.”

We are not seeing isolated, random attempts at attacks. We are witnessing the implementation of carefully orchestrated series of operations within the framework of a single plan. What is the main goal of the plan? To force the Russian troops to leave Ukraine.

Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent? The current Russian military doesn’t just seem incompetent — they are incompetent. And corrupt — from top to bottom. A Russian contract soldier who deserted and escaped to the West told about the disarray and corruption in the Russian army to Verstka Media. Anton (not his real name) decided to sign a contract with the Russian army to pay off the debts. Anton was struggling to repay loans amounting to 1 million ruble ($10,000). In Russia, most people don’t earn such money in a year. It were the bailiffs who convinced Anton to sign up for the war in Ukraine. Ads for army contract service are plastered all over Russia. (Stock photos are used throughout this post.) The conditions they offered sounded great: a contract with the civil organization JSC Investinform (it gets paid for recruiting soldiers for the war with Ukraine), plus the regional payout on sign up, plus payments from the Ministry of Defense. In total, Anton was supposed to be earning about 350,000 rub. per month ($3,500). In August 2023, Anton arrived in Moscow, signed a 1-year contract with the Ministry of Defense and an employment contract with JSC Investinform. The second contract allowed him to get top-up payments in addition to the standard 215,000 rub. ($2,150) MOD wage to Russian soldiers in Ukraine. That’s how Moscow officials meet the allocated quotas of soldiers per region: on paper, these recruits are Muscovites, but in reality, it’s deprived residents of small Russian towns living in poverty that are sent to the war. Muscovites have no desire to die for Putin; they live quite well. Think ‘Hunger Games’ districts and the Capitol: that’s Russia and Moscow. On sign up, Anton was immediately paid 400,000 rub. ($4,000). All debt collection proceedings against him had been suspended — that’s another “perk” offered to desperate Russians in need, to convince them to sign up for the war. However, he couldn’t use the money to repay the debts. Instead, he was forced to spend the money he got upfront to buy a proper uniform and personal protective equipment — bulletproof helmet, vest, etc. When new recruits arrived to the army training grounds, they were given some ancient uniforms and combat boots — all of them were 4–6 sizes too large. The helmet was from the times of WWII, a piece of shrapnel would pierce it like paper. But as soon as they arrived to barracks, helpful “intermediates” arrived, eager to sell to the fresh recruits all they needed. Nothing in the Russian army was for free. If you came to “earn big money”, you first needed to buy your own gear. The newbies had to pay the full retail price for their clothing and equipment. On top of that, they had to pay for parts for the machinery they would be using in the future. Some lame excuse was offered to make them pay for parts. Basically, commanders know how much cash you have been just paid, and extract it all before you have a chance to spend it. $4,000 went quick. The workers of the military warehouse where they were supposed to get equipment and uniforms were all drunk. Half of the officers were drunk as well. Quickly the recruits learned that they had to buy not only their own military gear but also food: within 2 weeks, all soldiers got food poisoning from eating the meals in the military canteen. So, they had to buy food in the local kiosk, where a liter of milk cost $8. The shop assistant was driving a luxury Mercedes, Anton says. Corruption in the Russian army is all-permeating. Because of Anton’s vocal complaints about the equipment, he was sent to a “Storm-Z” unit after the training course. Storm-Z is the “penal brigades”, where murderers and robbers recruited from prisons and deserters who were caught are shipped. Out of 600 recruits delivered to the front with him, only 40 survived after 2 months of assaults near Kupyansk. “It was just some kind of extermination. From one company, 5–6 people would return alive. The tanks and armored carriers were also smashed. In the end, we were mixed with prisoners and were simply pushed, pushed, pushed ahead.” How did he survive? “How I survived is a good question. I was a grenade launcher, not a stormtrooper, I didn’t go in attacks. We operated from hidden positions. Direct fire in these fields is not an option,” recalls Anton. “In 9 cases out of 10, storm troops are liquidated on approach.” “There are no experienced people in the infantry; people run away. If a person survives, he refuses to go on attacks, he starts having anxiety and hysterics. People rather go to jail than go on attacks.” In the village of Zaytsevo (Luhansk region), there is an unofficial jail where the Russians are holding soldiers who refused to continue to fight. Some of them say it’s “hell”, but it surely beats dying under heavy artillery fire trying to storm fortified Ukrainian positions. “The losses were simply insane, I lost count. For 3 kilometers, which were eventually taken back by the Ukrainians, 5–6 companies were killed,” According to Anton, the commanders are reprimanded for heavy losses, so all of those who haven’t returned from the attack are reported as “missing” (presumed deserters), not killed. Anton was deployed from the beginning of October till the end of November 2023. By that time, only a few people were left in his unit. They were taken in the rear of Russia-occupied Luhansk region, where they had to train the new recruits — prisoners and contractors. Then suddenly they were loaded on trucks and shipped to a camp in the Belgorod region (Russian territory near the border with Kharkiv region of Ukraine). By mid-March 2024, they were sent on the location near the Ukrainian border. Their unit was loaded on trucks (most Russian armed personnel carriers are destroyed by now, the troops are moved around by trucks) and for the whole night and the next day their column was driving on roads. Anton didn’t know that a raid by “Freedom of Russia Legion” was ongoing in the Belgorod region for already 3 days. He says that their commanders also didn’t know what was going on. Their trucks got under artillery fire. One of Anton’s colleagues was killed in a strike. His group hid at a cottage of a 90-year-old granny. No one knew what to do, commanders didn’t give any orders. They were under fire for several hours. Only the next morning the commanders contacted them and told them where to go. By that time, all locals escaped the village, stores and offices didn’t operate. The soldiers were ordered to stay in the local school, which was also closed. The soldiers simply hid there and slept. Communication with the base wasn’t working. They were under artillery fire, drones circling above the place. “We heard the conversations of our comrades, but we could not answer. There was an attack and breakthrough at their positions. Not only Storm-Z units were there but also border guards. In the meantime, it turned out that a whole platoon had been demolished in the woods.” Later the same day Anton went with a group to evacuate the wounded and dead from the battlefield — he had to replace the deceased colleague, although he hadn’t done evacuations before. During the evacuation, the group had to shed their weapons and armor, which weighed up to 50 kg, and walked 5 km back to the school. (The wounded guy that Anton evacuated died in the hospital.) In the basement, where the school canteen was, they took some sleep. As they woke up, they had to go back to get their weapons. Anton marked the location where he hid his grenade launcher on the map with an asterisk. “If I lost the grenade launcher, I would be transferred to the infantry, and infantry means certain death. Machine guns and rifles are dime a dozen, but it’s nearly impossible to procure something mightier.” Anton says that once his commander opened up and blurted: “I don’t give a f**k about you contractors, they’ll send me as many of you as I need — but for the lost equipment I would be hauled over the coals, it’s a lot of paperwork.” In storm troops, losses reach up to 90%, says Anton. He believes that if it weren’t for aerial bombing by the Russian Air Forces, the units of Russians that are fighting for Ukraine (“Freedom of Russia” Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, who were responsible for the raid on the Russian territory) would have easily captured the border areas of the Belgorod region with the help of FPV drones and artillery. Ukraine is superior to Russia by half a century in technical terms, their artillery is more accurate, and drones constantly conduct reconnaissance, Anton says. After the raid, the commander of Anton’s unit went on a drinking binge — along with his entire headquarters. The commander blamed the signalman for the failure in communications and began beating him up — after a few days of the torture, the signalman deserted. Meanwhile, Anton himself was thinking about doing the same thing. At the end of March 2024, he was watching a video of Russian oppositional channel ‘TV Dozhd’ (they were banned in Russia in 2022 and now broadcast from Europe), which mentioned the organization that helped Russian soldiers to escape the army and desert from the front (‘Idite Lesom’). At first he was skeptical, but when rumors about an upcoming offensive in the Kharkiv region spread, decided to give it a go. Anton says he realized that it’s impossible to survive in the Russian storm troops. Before agreeing to sign the contract, he had completely different ideas what it would be like. He asked the commanders to take 3 days off, but they refused. He couldn’t get a leave either — he says that even mobilized soldiers who serve since September 2022 can’t get a vacation. But he managed to get commanders’ permission to leave the unit for 1 night — until the morning. “Almost everyone who has been behind the front line thinks about escaping,” says Anton. 1.5 months after his escape, he cannot adapt to the peaceful life in a safe European country. Sometimes he has panic attacks and adrenaline rushes, but he tries to suppress them. His attitude towards the war in Ukraine has changed greatly. “There is guilt on me,” admits Anton. ”Once, our detachment commander broke down, drunk: “Yes, we are f***ing orcs!” “It’s disillusionment. The commanders don’t show it, and such coming outs happen mainly because they are drunk. During my time there, my entire outlook on life changed. I no longer feel anything positive about the Russian state. This is not a war, but some kind of agony. The only parallels that emerge are with the World War 1. We are simply being sent to slaughter,” concludes Anton. He plans to stay in Europe and apply for political asylum. He believes that he has the right to claim it as “a person who refused to participate in war crimes.” He never fully repaid the loans — and has no plans to do it.

Why does Russia refuse to accept equal blame for the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and the start of WWII? On August 23, 1939, two criminal regimes — organizers of World War 2, Germany and the Soviet Union, signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and its secret protocol, defining the split of European territories between them. The pact gave the final impetus to the new world war, which began just 8 days later, with Germany’s attack on Poland. Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact: German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop (left), Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and USSR Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov (right) on August 23, 1939 in the Kremlin after signing the pact. Stalin made a toast after the ceremony: "I know how much the German people love their Fuhrer. Therefore, I want to drink to his health." On September 1, 1939 Germany’s attacked Poland. The Soviet Union attacked Poland on September 17, 1939. On September 22, Nazis and Soviets held a joint parade in Brest, celebrating their victory. For 50 years, the USSR leaders denied that there was a secret appendix to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. In 1946, at the Nuremberg Trials, the former State Secretary of the German Foreign Ministry, Ernst von Weizsäcker, spoke about the existence of a secret additional protocol between the USSR and Germany. This was confirmed by other defendants, and one of the lawyers even wanted to read the text of this protocol, but he was not allowed: the USSR representatives called it a fake and said such a document never existed. In 1948, the secret protocol, based on photocopies of the German original that had not survived, was published in the US State Department collection "Nazi-Soviet Relations. 1939-1941". It also included the correspondence between Nazi and Soviet diplomats, which contained references to secret agreements. But the Soviet Union continued to claim that this was a falsification, that no additional secret appendix to the 1939 agreements ("On Non-Aggression" and "On Friendship and Borders") between the USSR and Germany existed. Moreover: in response to the publication by the State Department, Moscow published its own work titled "Falsifiers of History". But it did not contain a single complete copy of a document, only a few fragments. Stalin didn’t want to be blamed in starting the World War with Hitler, and used the status of the USSR as one of the “victors of WW2” to suppress this extremely important information. Molotov, who signed the non-aggression pact and the secret protocol to it, denied its existence until his death in 1986. Minister of Foreign Affairs of the USSR Vyacheslav Molotov in Berlin, November 14, 1940. It was hard to prove that such a document existed: one party that signed it (Hitler's Germany) no longer existed, and the other (the Soviet Union) denied that it existed at all, and had no intention of publishing it. Only in 1989, the Soviet leaders admitted that such secret protocol existed, on request of representatives of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. A copy of the German document was published in the USSR. The actual copy of the secret protocol in Russian was first kept in Stalin's safe and then in the archive of the Central Committee of the Communist Party. In 1992, after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the archive of the Communist Party was declassified and the secret protocol was discovered. From that moment, the existence of a secret additional treaty to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact had become a reliably recognized fact not only in the West, not only in the Baltic countries, Moldova and Ukraine, but also in Russia itself. But now, Putin’s propaganda downplays the importance of the secret agreement between Hitler and Stalin how they would divide Europe, and overemphasizes that it was a non-aggression pact, which allowed the USSR 2 more years without the war. Completely disregarding the fact that without the secret agreement to split European lands, there possibly wouldn’t happen such a war. Putin went much further than Stalin — he now claims it was Russia that defeated Hitler (not even the USSR but Russia), and the whole world must be grateful to Russia for defeating the Nazi regime. Putin’s propaganda promoted this idea for years, having convinced some westerners that Russia was some kind of “savior” nation. And then Putin used this notion to attack Ukraine: he labeled Ukrainians “Nazis” and sent the Russian troops to invade Ukraine “to defeat a Neo-Nazi regime”. Putin hoped it would work and the world would buy into it. He still hopes he can convince us.

What was it like in the USSR between the 1991 coup d'état attempt and the dissolution of the Soviet Union? The August 1991 coup by ‘GKChP’ (State Committee on Emergency Situation) — formed by die-hard communists who were against democratic changes introduced by the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev — shocked the USSR citizens to the core. In these 3 days from August 19 to 21 people feared that their newfound freedoms — most notably, freedom of private entrepreneurship and freedom of speech — would be again taken away from them by the communists. This is why thousands of people came to the central squares of the cities — to defend what they’ve just got. People liked the new life more than the old, pre-1985 life. When the coup was defeated and its participants arrested, people breathed a sigh of relief. But their problems didn’t disappear. There was still shortage of food in the country. December 14, 1991, ‘In The Queue’ (independent newspaper): “Ukraine sends ham and sugar to Russia. The government of the capital begins to privatize shops. There will be no hunger — there will be enough potatoes and flour for the whole of winter.” This newspaper was published 6 days after the Belovezha Accords were signed on December 8, 1991, declaring that the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) had effectively ceased to exist. On December 12, the Supreme Soviet of the Russian SFSR formally ratified the Belovezha Accords, denounced the 1922 Treaty on the Creation of the Soviet Union, and recalled the Russian deputies from the Supreme Soviet of the USSR. GKChP sped up the process of the Soviet republics wanting to separate from the abusive treatment by Moscow. But the leaders of Russia (which was only 1 of 15 Soviet Republics) also didn’t want the USSR anymore — and the Soviet people were weary of the return of “the classic communism”. That’s why no one really cared when the USSR ceased to exist. It was strange, weird, yet kind of unimportant — the important people, like leaders of each republic, were still on charge. So, people just moved on with their lives, without thinking twice, and started to get ready to celebrate Christmas and the New Year’s Eve. The giant 70-year-old country stopped existing — and people carried on, as of nothing happened. That was truly remarkable.

NATO is running low on weapons and stockpiles. They can barely muster enough tanks that will last all of 1 month. Russia is in full industrial swing and amassing over 500K troops at the border. What are some weird facts about the USSR and living in the Communist Soviet Union? At least 1.1 million people have been executed by Stalin’s regime during the Great Purge in 1937–1938. The purpose of the purge was to destroy any possible resistance to the totalitarian Soviet regime ruled by Joseph Stalin. These are the photos taken by the NKVD, the Soviet secret service, of innocent people they were about to execute. All the people in these photos were shot in basements after confessing under torture in various heinous crimes — spying for Japan, China or France, plotting to assassinate Stalin, and so on. All the people in these photos were “rehabilitated” after Stalin’s death (declared innocent). The families of those shot didn’t know their loved ones were dead. For years, they were sending them parcels with food, cigarettes, warm clothing — when they themselves didn’t have enough to eat and wore the same clothes for years. The relatives of the victims were coming to the department of prisons and standing in queues for hours to send parcels, tolerating abuse and mockery from the guards. You don’t need to guess where the contents of these parcels went. It’s only after Stalin’s death they found out that the sentence of “10 years without correspondence” meant that the person was shot on the same day. In addition to 1.1 million people who were shot, 4.5 million of USSR citizens were sent to remote GULAG camps for terms of minimum of 10 years, sentenced to hard labor. Many of them died before they got there — getting sick in cattle train carriages, during long marches to the “camps”, many others died later in the camps because of deceases, starvation, freezing cold, exhaustion, or took their own lives. Women often were raped to death on arrival to a prison camp, after a queue of hardened male prisoners were given access by prison guards in exchange for a pack of cigarettes. Meanwhile, the rest of Soviet citizens pretended that nothing was happening, that life was great, and becoming better with every year. The black NKVD cars were arriving at night and quickly grabbing the whole family, by morning the apartment was empty, as if no one ever lived there. And the neighbors weren’t asking questions because they didn’t want the black car to pick them up the next night. That’s the country that Vladimir Putin wants to restore.
