Reportedly, only 4 city beaches are open throughout Moscow. The rest are closed “for reconstruction” or due to poor water quality. The hot days in Russia prompted a spike in drownings: people flock to water, but many overestimate their swimming ability — and there are hundreds of drownings. In Chuvashia, the top prosecutor Andrei Fomin drowned on July 1, while taking part in ‘Chebswim’ race. Presumably, Fomin became unwell during the swimming race. He was pulled out of the water by rescuers and handed over to doctors, but they could not revive him. 57-year-old Fomin headed the prosecutor's office of Chuvashia since April 2020. Until 2014, he worked in the Yaroslavl region, where he was born, but after the annexation of Crimea, Fomin was appointed the deputy prosecutor of Crimea, and worked there until 2020. ‘Chebswim’ competition is held on the Volga River, and anyone can take part in it. The river is quite wide at that point: participants can cross the river one way (2200 m) or return (4400 m). Russians’ propensity for getting drunk near water (aka “relaxing in nature”) and traditional disregard for the rules (people swim even at the places where signs “swimming prohibited” are plastered) are behind the growing number of summer drownings. According to the official data, 1,439 people have drowned in Russia in 2024 — 201 of them were kids. Nobody really cares.

How many casualties has Russia suffered? Moscow region increased the one-off payout on signup for the willing cannon fodder for the Ukrainian war — these willing to play the death lottery are now offered 1.9 million ruble (around USD $22,000). In addition, there is the federal payout of 225,000 rub., bringing the total premium to $24,000 per head. The move is caused by plunging numbers of volunteers — and each region must deliver a certain number of soldiers per year, on Putin’s orders. The typical volunteer recruit comes from depressed regional towns of Russia — of which there are tens of thousands. Muscovites live reasonably well, the city life is at full swing, no one is interested in dying to stop mythical Nazis in Ukraine. Thus, raids on migrants to send these with Russian passports to the army, and pressurize illegals to sign the contract under the threat of imprisonment. But that’s still not enough. This is why the Russian state constantly raises the one-off payments for signing the army contract, which make it feasible for poor Russians from regions to travel to Moscow to sign up. Recruiters lie and tell aspiring high-wage-earners that they would be “safeguarding warehouses in the rear” or “digging trenches”. But when they arrive to Ukraine — after a 2-week stunt at a training camp (where most recruits mostly drink and hang out with newly made friends) — they are simply shipped to the front trenches and given a gun, and told to hold positions. Under a heavy fire. And there is no one to complain to. But even with all the tricks and money on offer, Russia can only deliver about 25,000-30,000 new recruits monthly, which isn’t enough to replenish the heavy losses. By the end of July 2024, the losses of the Russian army reached over 570,000 personnel, killed and wounded. Russia’s average daily losses in the last 2 months exceed 1,000 personnel daily. In Kazan, a referral fee of 100,000 ruble ($1,150) is paid to those who bring a friend to the military registration office to sign up for the war in Ukraine. A friend in need is a friend indeed. Other regions are also raising payouts on signup for the war. Russia is struggling to maintain the numbers at the front, and the only thing that worked before to get volunteers — money — is losing its appeal.

Do you think it is fair to call a westerner who supports Putin’s invasion and actively spreads Putinist propaganda in comment sections, a quisling? Well, Moldova aren’t just calling the citizens who spread Putin’s propaganda a “quisling” (“traitor”) — they are amending the criminal code to prosecute spreading disinformation in the interests of other states as treason. The term “quisling” arose because in World War II, Vidkun Quisling, a Norwegian politician, volunteered to help the occupying Nazis rule Norway for Germany. Now the term is used to mean a traitor, especially one who collaborates with an enemy occupying force for personal gain. Quisling was arrested and tried for war crimes in 1945, and sentenced to death. He was executed on October 24, 1945. The parliamentary majority (PAS party of Moldova President Maia Sandu) proposed to expand the legal definition treason by adding another type of activity: “assisting a foreign state, foreign organization, anti-constitutional entity or their representatives to carry out hostile activities against the security of the state”. This would include, in particular, “carrying out disinformation campaigns, organized activities aimed at achieving hostile goals through disinformation, which may harm the sovereignty, independence, unity, indivisibility, security or defense capacity of the Republic of Moldova.” Russia is de-facto occupying 17% of the territory of Moldova — the areas called Transnistria and Gagauzia, since 1990s. Russia claims that Moldova violates the rights of the Russian population of these self-proclaimed “republics” (you probably never knew about their existence until today). Sounds familiar?
